item.title: ‘Jeremiah’s to lose’ – Heisman Trophy rankings on social media spark interesting discussion
item.description: Photo by Kirk Irwin/Getty Images Despite Jeremiah Smith being the frontrunner for the Heisman Trophy this year, a ranking of the top 10 players competing for the award has led to some interesting online discourse. Jeremiah Smith has emerged as the frontrunner in the 2026 Heisman Trophy race, putting up 984 receiving yards and 12 touchdowns in seven games for Ohio State. The Buckeyes star is chasing history as he looks to become the first wide receiver to win the award since DeVonta Smith in 2020. It is never that simple, though. Miami quarterback Darian Mensah and Ole Miss man Trinidad Chambliss are putting together strong cases of their own. Other names like Notre Dame’s CJ Carr and Georgia’s Gunner Stockton have also been thrown around before, but they haven’t made this list. Football fans say Jeremiah Smith is the frontrunner but the competition is heating up Seven weeks into the season, lots of teams are enjoying strong starts, thanks to some of the stars who are looking to win the Heisman. The Rebels’ success has been attributed to Chambliss, while the Tennessee Volunteers’ wins have seen DeSean Bishop enter the conversation. On Monday, On3 shared their rankings for the top 10 college players in contention for the award, and fans responded to the list with some expected takes, but also some truly unique ones. “We appreciate the Bishop recognition. He deserves to be in the conversation,” one fan wrote. “It’s Jeremiah’s award to lose, but awesome to see Jesse Legree getting some national love,” a second fan said. “Trinidad should be number one after Saturday’s performance,” claimed a third fan. “Braden deserves to be higher than 10, but thrilled to see TWO Beavers on this list!” one comment said. “How is Conner Weigman not on here?” a fifth fan asked. “This graphic doesn’t properly illustrate how big the gap is between Jeremiah and the field,” another fan wrote. “I know everyone wants to give it to Jeremiah already, but I think many others deserve recognition too,” a seventh fan commented. Smith remains the frontrunner, but a lot can change over the course of the season. The field looks stacked for this year’s Heisman Trophy, and the race will be one to watch. Will Jeremiah claim the award as many think he will? Only time and a lot of football will tell. item.title: Roma maintain best defensive record in Europe
item.description: Roma maintain best defensive record in Europe No one in Europe has conceded fewer goals than Roma. Before last night, the Giallorossi were joined by Cagliari, but the incredible 4-0 defeat against Monza has sent the Sardinians plummeting in the standings. Mancini and his teammates have conceded only three goals: two against Inter and one against Atalanta. In the top five European leagues, Lazio and Borussia Dortmund are hot on Roma’s heels with four. Their defensive solidity hasn’t diminished even after Svilar’s injury. Gollini has already kept two clean sheets in Serie A against Como and Genoa. Gasperini calls his defenders ‘gladiators’, and he’s right. Hermoso, for example, is third in Serie A for interceptions per game (2.4). Ndicka is eighth for defensive closures per game (5.8). After a difficult start to the season, Mancini is returning to his best form, and this year Balerdi and Koulierakis have joined him. The Argentine is already a key player and a true all-rounder. He can play in all three positions in the three-man defense, and tonight against Slovan he’ll lead the defense. Ghilardi is getting less time, but as the matchdays go by, he’ll also get more minutes. The Giallorossi wall continues to impress.

Her performance was dominant and demonstrative. Reese had 30 points and 16 rebounds in the win. She did it her way. Demanding the ball from her teammates, snarling at the crowd and letting everyone in Ballhalla know a defender who could contain her wasn’t in the building. item.title: Six of the best free transfers in Premier League history
item.description: Six of the best free transfers in Premier League history In an era when Premier League clubs routinely shatter transfer records, a successful free transfer can still represent outstanding business. Jean-Marc Bosman helped change football forever with the landmark ruling that bears his name in 1995. Free transfers have since delivered some of the Premier League’s most memorable bargains. Best free transfers in Premier League history Ruud Gullit - Chelsea (1995) Some signings can transform a club's image entirely, and Ruud Gullit fits that brief. The Ballon d'Or winner pitched up in West London in the mid-nineties, at a time when Chelsea found themselves perennially marooned in mid-table. Gullit made an immediate impression and finished runner-up for the 1995/96 FWA Footballer of the Year award, with the Dutch icon's impact paving the path for an eclectic collection of overseas stars, such as Gianluca Vialli and Gianfranco Zola, to head to Stamford Bridge. Sol Campbell - Arsenal (2001) Arguably the best free-transfer signing in Premier League history, and certainly one of its most controversial. There was genuine astonishment when Arsene Wenger paraded Sol Campbell as Arsenal 's latest signing, with the Gunners having swooped to sign the England defender from bitter rivals Tottenham. Campbell had his choice of Europe's top teams, but instead opted for a controversial defection across North London. Campbell helped Arsenal to a domestic double in his debut season, and was part of the club's Invincible title winners in 2004. Okocha had flicks, tricks, and a spectacular goal collection during four fun-filled seasons in English football. item.title: Paris FC president Pierre Ferracci announces departure
item.description: Paris FC president Pierre Ferracci announces departure Pierre Ferracci announced that he will leave his position as president of Paris FC. His exit was already anticipated for the end of the season, however, it has been brought forward. Ferracci made the announcement during an event on Monday. He will become an honorary president, whilst Antoine Arnault, the representative of the owners, the Arnault family, will succeed Ferracci. The decision must be ratified by the Administration Council, which is set to sit next on 9th November. The match against AS Monaco at the Stade Jean Bouin on 1st November is expected to be his last. An hommage is planned. As well as vacating his role, Ferracci will also part ways with his shares. His 28.9% share will go to Agache Sport, the sporting subsidiary of LVMH, the majority shareholder. Red Bull still possesses a 10.6% share. “It is the right time for me to pass the torch,” said Ferracci on Monday in a speech transcribed by L’Équipe . He leaves the position with Paris FC third in Ligue 1 and level with leaders Olympique Lyonnais. GFFN | Luke Entwistle

item.title: 'There are no limits!' - Ambitious Charlie Cresswell talks up Rennes Europa League chances as he chases England dream
item.description: FBL-FRA-LIGUE1-RENNES-AUXERRE - AFP English defender embraces French adventure Cresswell has expressed supreme confidence in his new side's European prospects while harbouring clear ambitions of breaking into the England senior squad. The centre-back opted to move across the Channel in 2024 by joining Toulouse after making just 14 appearances for boyhood club Leeds. He subsequently moved to Rennes on loan in the summer of 2026, with the French outfit agreeing an initial €2.5 million deal featuring an obligation to make the transfer permanent next year for €22.5m plus bonuses. Bold move accelerates career progression Bold move accelerates career progression Leaving his comfort zone proved immensely beneficial after he established himself as a central figure in France, starting 57 out of a possible 68 Ligue 1 games across two seasons at Toulouse. Despite interest from Brighton over a potential return to England last summer, discussions with his partner cemented his decision to join Rennes - a club previously represented by former Leeds team-mates Raphinha, Joe Rodon, and Glen Kamara, as well as ex-England Under-21 colleague Djed Spence. item.title: ‘It’s Frustrating,’ ‘It Starts With Me’ — Valkyries’ Natalie Nakase, Veronica Burton Address Game 2 Turnover Nightmare vs. Angel Reese’s Dream
item.description: Collage featuring BASKETBALL-WNBA-LV-GSV/, BASKETBALL-WNBA-GSV-ATL/, and BASKETBALL-WNBA-LV-GSV/. IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Golden State Valkyries suffered a 79-65 loss to the Atlanta Dream in WNBA Finals Game 2, with the team’s turnovers becoming a major problem. After committing a season-high 18 turnovers, coach Natalie Nakase and guard Veronica Burton took responsibility for the mistakes as Atlanta tied the series 1-1 behind Angel Reese’s historic performance. Natalie Nakase, Veronica Burton Address Valkyries’ Turnover Problems After Game 2 Loss Golden State’s ball security took a sharp turn for the worse on Monday. The Valkyries had committed just 8 turnovers in their 68-64 Game 1 win, but that number jumped to 18 in Game 2. It was also well above their regular-season average of 10.4 turnovers per game. Atlanta made them pay, scoring 24 points off those mistakes. The Dream’s aggressive defense disrupted Golden State’s passing lanes and forced players into rushed decisions, helping Atlanta take control of the game. During her post-match presser, Nakase acknowledged that her team could have done a better job protecting the ball, while giving credit to the Dream for the pressure they applied. “It’s controllable. It’s definitely controllable,” Nakase said of the turnovers . “I thought they did a great job sprinting back, getting into the gaps, getting into the driving lanes. So just credit to them on their effort, their hustle, their fight.” DON’T MISS: ‘We Felt Embarrassed’ — Angel Reese Doesn’t Mince Words After Historic Performance Fuels Dream’s Bounce-Back in WNBA Finals Game 2 The Valkyries were also beaten in an area central to their identity, something the 46-year-old coach admitted was frustrating. “It’s frustrating, right? That’s been part of our identity is because our identity is defense. We hang our hats on that,” she said. Nakase added that she planned to review the team’s performance and question whether she had communicated the game plan clearly enough. Burton, who averaged 5.7 assists and 1.5 turnovers per game during the regular season, was equally direct about her own role in the problem. The starting guard, who had 3 turnovers in this game, accepted that she needed to be more careful with the ball and help the team stay organized. “That’s what they’re known for, and we’re known for the opposite. So, I mean, it starts with me,” Burton said . “Like, I can’t just be throwing the ball.” She also pointed to hesitation and players being out of sync as reasons for the mistakes, saying the team needed to be more decisive and get on the same page. Center Kiah Stokes echoed that assessment, noting that Atlanta raised its defensive pressure and Golden State failed to execute consistently. Golden State could not find their usual rhythm, and their mistakes gave the Dream more chances to score in transition. item.title: Lowry joins McIlroy in first ever TGL Trade
item.description: [Getty Images] Shane Lowry is the first player to be traded in the TMRW Golf League (TGL) and will join Rory McIlroy at Boston Common Golf for 2027. Ireland's Lowry makes the move before the third season of TGL, which takes place at the SoFi Centre in Florida and comprises traditional golf with technology. The 39-year-old spent the first two seasons at The Bay GC, and he will now link up with five-time major winner McIlroy as team rosters expand to five players for the new campaign. USA Ryder Cup captain Keegan Bradley and Masters champions Adam Scott and Hideki Matsuyama joined McIlroy at Boston Common Golf last season. In a trade for Lowry, The Bay will acquire Boston Common Golf's fourth draft selection to fill its open roster spot, as well as one future selection over the next three seasons and commercial considerations. McIlroy, who co-founded TGL alongside Tiger Woods and Mike McCarley, said 2019 Open champion Lowry is a "great friend" and he loves playing alongside him. "We've had some special wins together, including at the Zurich Classic, and I know the quality of his game and how much he cares about winning for his team-mates," he added. "I'm delighted to welcome him to Boston Common Golf and excited about what we can achieve together this season." Lowry, who won the Irish Open at Doonbeg in September, added he was "delighted" to make the move to link up with McIlroy for the new campaign. "Having Rory alongside me and being part of this group makes it particularly exciting, and I'm looking forward to helping the team bring a championship to Boston," he said. Elsewhere in the league, new team Motor City Golf Club announced five-time major winner Brooks Koepka as its first player.

item.title: MotoGP teams told Qatar Grand Prix expected to go ahead
item.description: Motorsport photo The MotoGP Teams Association has informed teams that it intends to press ahead with the Qatar Grand Prix in three weeks’ time, despite the volatile situation in the Middle East. The race, originally scheduled for April, was postponed until the 6-8 November following the outbreak of war in Iran in late February. The conflict remains ongoing and most European countries are advising their citizens to postpone any travel to Qatar, even though the situation is no longer as intense as it was during the initial stages. However, MotoGP Sports Entertainment Group (MGPSEG), the championship promoter, considers the assurances it has received from the Qatari authorities and the local promoter sufficient to guarantee the event’s safety. The race is due to be the third leg of a triple-header comprising the Australian Grand Prix next weekend and the Malaysian round the following week. With 15 days to go before the MotoGP paddock is due to be set up at the Lusail circuit on the outskirts of the capital Doha, the International Road-Racing Teams Association (IRTA) has emailed all teams to inform them of its intention to hold the race. In the message, IRTA stresses that the local promoter has developed a specific contingency plan, which is complemented by the advice MGPSEG is receiving. The body representing the teams also makes clear that it is in contact with relevant embassies. According to the communication, none of them has advised a change of approach. Over the past few weeks, the teams have held numerous meetings with the championship’s senior executives, who have consistently reiterated their intention to stage the race. In this respect, it is worth highlighting the change of position adopted by Yamaha and Honda, the two Japanese manufacturers, which were initially firmly opposed to sending anyone to a conflict zone. Yamaha’s case is particularly significant: almost two months ago, the tuning-fork brand instructed its logistics staff to look for alternative flight routes for all its personnel to avoid travelling through the affected region. It remains to be seen what measures the companies involved in the championship will take, given that their internal policies prohibit employees from travelling to territories considered unstable. The riders, meanwhile, are divided between those who are wary of having to travel to Doha, who make up the vast majority, and those who have expressed no reservations about going. Motorsport.com understands that three-quarters of the grid would prefer to avoid racing there, while the remaining quarter is in favour of going ahead with the race. item.title: Manchester United and Liverpool battling for Borussia Dortmund star
item.description: Manchester United and Liverpool battling for Borussia Dortmund star Manchester United and Liverpool are both considering a move for Borussia Dortmund midfielder Felix Nmecha, according to TEAMtalk. The report suggests that Manchester United have made contact as they assess their options ahead of the winter transfer window. Meanwhile, Liverpool reportedly see the 26-year-old as a potential alternative to Bournemouth’s Alex Scott. Chelsea, Tottenham, Newcastle United, Manchester City and Arsenal have also previously been linked with Nmecha. A winter transfer appears highly unlikely, but Dortmund would be powerless to prevent a move if a club triggers Nmecha’s €80 million release clause in the summer, before it expires at the end of June. Nmecha’s contract with Dortmund runs until 2030.

item.title: Frankfurt to look at Germany and their own academy for new players
item.description: Markus Kroesche (R), outgoing board member for sport of Eintracht Frankfurt, and CEO of Eintracht Frankfurt Axel Hellmann attend Eintracht Frankfurt's general meeting at the Jahrhunderthalle. (is associated with: «Frankfurt to look at Germany and their own academy for new players») Florian Wiegand/dpa Eintracht Frankfurt plan to find new players on the German market and in their own academy in the future to be less dependent on transfer income for foreign players they have developed. Club president Matthias Beck told the club assembly on Monday night that while they want to continue playing for European berths "the path towards that will have to see adaptations based on economic reason. "Our focus will be more on the German market and our academy," Beck said. The change coincide with the departure of board member for sport Markus Krösche, who made a name for himself by bringing talented foreign players to the club and selling them on for big fees during his five years. They include Hugo Ekitiké, who went to Liverpool for €100 million ($112.4 million), the €90 million sale of Randal Kolo Muani to Paris Saint-Germain and Omar Marmoush's €75 million move to Manchester City. During Krösche's tenure Frankfurt won the Europa League in 2022 and came third in the Bundesliga in 2025. They failed to qualify for Europe in the past season and have also had a slow start into the new campaign. New CEO Axel Hellmann has said that "the business model we moved in has changed," partly because the rich Premier League has made its latest big transfers mainly on the domestic English market and not abroad. "The approach of deliberately focusing on developing young players in order to make financial progress no longer works to the same extent as it did in previous years,” Hellmann said. “We must systematically reduce our financial dependence on transfer fees and make a greater effort to base our financial stability on the revenue generated within this region." Hellmann said the club intends to “look more closely at the youth academy, look more closely at Germany and look more closely at potential German internationals.” “This is not a departure from our approach, but rather an adjustment that takes account of the fact that the fundamental conditions of the market have changed.”

item.title: Urban Meyer calls out ‘perplexing’ Ohio State’s Ryan Day QB decision
item.description: Adam Cairns/Columbus Dispatch / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images Urban Meyer calls out ‘perplexing’ Ohio State’s Ryan Day QB decision appeared first on ClutchPoints . Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here . The Ohio State football team is going to play multiple games without their starting quarterback, Julian Sayin, who suffered an injury during their win against Indiana. Backup quarterback Luke Fahey is in line to lead the offense of Ryan Day ’s team, but former football head coach Urban Meyer believes five-star quarterback Tavien St. Clair should receive an opportunity to showcase his abilities. On The Triple Option, Meyer expressed his confusion over St. Clair’s limited role and shared why Ohio State must prioritize preparing its backup quarterbacks during the bye week. “It’s perplexing why he’s not the quarterback, and you know why he doesn’t jog on the field,” Meyer said. “Let’s say he went down. We went through this, obviously, so I came to the Cardinal Jones. You know everyone else is kind of tired. Everyone else is kind of, but you have to practice your ass off.” Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial) “And I would talk to the team we did and apologize to the players. Normally, it’s the time to rest, guys. And you’ll rest some. In my understanding, Ohio State’s got a very unselfish team. They’re going to go practice as much this week and get their backup quarterback ready because you’ve got a real one coming up. I’m curious to see if they try the five-star.” Sayin suffered the injury late in the fourth quarter against Indiana. Before leaving the game, he completed 15 of 29 pass attempts for 235 yards and two touchdowns, though he also threw two interceptions. Then Fahey stepped in for Sayin against Indiana. The timing of Sayin’s injury makes Ohio State’s quarterback decision particularly significant, as the team has a bye week to prepare before facing USC. The Buckeyes entered the bye week with a 6-1 record following their win over Indiana. However, maintaining that momentum without Sayin will require adjustments from the coaching staff. Day must now decide whether to continue trusting the established backup in Fahey or allow the five-star St. Clair to take control of Ohio State’s offense. Liverpool were told, in effect, that the bright lights called louder. Now the same player is staring at a team sheet and finding Federico Valverde in his lane. You could not script it better. That said, football has never been a monastery. Sentiment matters, but quality matters more. If Liverpool genuinely believe Trent Alexander-Arnold improves the side, then the only serious question is whether the numbers stack up and whether the dressing room would embrace it. The rest is noise from people who enjoy performing outrage on demand. There would be grumbles, of course. Some would call it a step too far. Some would mutter about loyalty and badges and all the old hymns. Then the first whipped pass into the box lands on a sixpence, a forward buries it, and half the moral panic melts into applause. That is football. It remembers everything and forgives more than it admits. If he comes back, he comes back to prove a point. If he stays in Madrid, Liverpool move on. item.title: PREVIEW: Wolves face Portsmouth for the first time since 2010
item.description: PREVIEW: Wolves face Portsmouth for the first time since 2010 Portsmouth will travel to Molineux on Tuesday evening for the first time in 17 years to face Wolves in a rescheduled Championship fixture. With a game in hand, a win for Cesar Peixoto’s side will see them return to the top five of the Championship table, having amassed 17 points from 10 matches so far this term. Wolves claimed a 2-1 victory over Burnley last time out, thanks to goals from Fer Lopez and Tawanda Chirewa, giving the Old Gold all three points. Meanwhile, Portsmouth sit 13th in the table, but John Mousinho’s side come into this fixture in good form, having won their last two games, a 3-2 victory against Sheffield United and a 1-0 win over Norwich on the weekend. Lopez has made a fantastic start to the 2026/27 season at Wolves, with the young midfielder being one to watch tomorrow night after scoring five and assisting twice in 10 matches. Ebou Adams has emerged as a standout performer for Portsmouth this season, scoring twice and assisting once, and leading in tackles and defensive contributions. Following his MCL injury against Everton, Wolves director of performance, Phil Hayward, has confirmed that Raul Jimenez will undergo surgery on his knee, ruling the Mexican striker out of the squad until at least January. Other notable admissions include Rodrigo Gomes and Adam Armstrong, who will both miss tomorrow night’s clash through injury. For Pompey, it’s a long list of injuries, with Keshi Anderson expected to be sidelined for up to two months of action following their 3-2 victory over Sheffield United, according to Mousinho. This is the first meeting between the clubs since May 2010, with Pompey being unbeaten in their past six visits to Molineux, five of which ended in draws. The match is due to take place at 7:45 pm BST on Tuesday night and will be broadcast live on Sky Sports.

item.description: [BBC] [Shutterstock] Three games in a week, nine points, three clean sheets - this is not typical Blues. Being a football fan is an odd thing; when things are going well, you move away from your usual state of depression into worrying about when the bubble is going to burst. I will therefore put my natural pessimism aside and try to enjoy our purple patch. Liam Millar has now clocked up seven goal involvements in seven games and I am hoping there is an option to get him on a permanent basis like we did with Patrick Roberts last season. His contributions on Saturday were one of the highlights of an excellent team performance. To be honest, I had been eyeing this game as a tough one compared to Tuesday night's against Preston, as it was fourth v fifth and we were level on points with QPR. As it was, their attacking outlets found themselves limited; Paul Smyth was muscled out of the game by Bright Osayi-Samuel, and the Christoph Klarer-Phil Neumann brick wall was very effective in limiting Kwame Poku and Rayan Kolli. I also need to give a couple of other shout-outs to members of the team, first to Tomoki Iwata. He has been the subject of grumbling from some Blues fans, but set up both of Millar's goals and is playing some really good football at the moment. Secondly, to Jay Stansfield. He is instrumental in the way Blues play the press, forcing opposition players into mistakes, such as the one that led to our first goal on Saturday. Demarai Gray's stoppage-time goal was a thing of beauty, and the icing on the cake for this week. Right now, Blues are operating really well. Players like Millar are being allowed to play with freedom and we seem to have taken a big step away from the 'possession but no outlet' football of last season that many fans were frustrated by. Chris Davies did say he had learnt some lessons and so far, he is doing well putting them into practice. It is a thumbs-up from me. item.title: Dwight Yorke: ‘I’m not a kid trying to get into management – I’m a manager’
item.description: Ghana may soon come calling for Trinidad and Tobago’s former captain and manager, who is proud of his CV since his days as a Premier League striker Dwight Yorke wants you to stop calling him a former player. “I’m not a kid trying to get into management for the first time,” he says from his home in Dubai. “I’ve done that and I want that message to come across clearly.” The message has a deadline. Carlos Queiroz left his job as Ghana head coach on 1 October and the Ghana Football Association is searching for his successor. item.title: Brighton are the apex B club – their next target should be a Champions League place | Jonathan Wilson
item.description: Diego Gómez’s wondergoal in a five-star demolition is just the latest in an impressive run of results for the south coast team Sign up for our free newsletter here For two or three years now, it’s been standard to nod approvingly at how well-run Brighton, Brentford and Bournemouth are, and to move on. What else is there to say? It’s true, of course – these are sides who have made the most of relatively limited resources. But there’s also an underlying assumption in the designation: that these are clubs who have no higher aspiration, that their limit is earning praise for upper mid-table finishes. This season, perhaps, offers an opportunity to change that. Other than Arsenal, every major club is undergoing significant transition. Manchester City may have started the season with seven straight wins, but there’s every chance the punishment for their multiple breaches of Premier League regulations takes them out of the race for the top five. In that context, why shouldn’t one of those efficient smaller sides qualify for the Champions League? Continue reading...

item.title: Bayern and Luis Díaz warm up for Arsenal revenge mission with furious rout of Leipzig | Andy Brassell
item.description: Bruised Bundesliga champions hit a supposed rival for six and their flying winger is peaking at a perfect moment When Bayern Munich fail to win for two games in a row, you know what is coming next. Particularly on a Saturday night showcase, against the sort of good domestic opposition that tend to bring the best out of the champions. It had been a frustrating week, domestically and continentally, in two games on the road. On both occasions they had been caught cold, conceding the Bundesliga’s fastest goal at Augsburg and going 1-0 down in less than 90 seconds in Stavanger . Vincent Kompany’s low profile on the Allianz Arena touchline, almost motionless in his seat as his team rattled a flurry of goals past poor RB Leipzig, had nothing to do with any lingering chagrin connected to those slow starts from his team. The sporting director, Max Eberl, who stood in for his coach in the post-match press conference, explained that the Belgian had been ill, not to mention Kompany’s current hip problem that had made the move from dressing room to pitchside slow and uncomfortable. item.title: Europe is a blast – but more a curse than a blessing if you are not a Premier League super-club I Jonathan Wilson
item.description: The four Premier League clubs playing in the lesser continental competitions face each other on Sunday – but three are struggling domestically The sun shone. The temperature was in the high 20s. There was a mood of great conviviality. If you were struggling with the official allocation, it turned out you could just email the president of Torreense and he’d sort you out. Were these “Nuno-tickets” real? It turned out they were. Not only that, but you could sit anywhere you wanted in a stadium too big for the game and, if you happened to have gravitated to the comfortable hospitality seating at the back of the lower tier, the beer was inexplicably free. Locals in Leiria seemed bewildered but could hardly have been more accommodating. A beer pump had been installed outside a patisserie on the Praça Francisco Rodrigues Lobo, whose owner soon found fans happy to help stack empty barrels if that facilitated the free flow of Sagres. “There was a meeting at the town hall to explain these are not hooligans,” said the owner of a radical leftist flammkuchen restaurant between the square and the cathedral. “They told us the club comes from the labour movement and I found that very interesting.” And how had she found the fans? “Noisy, but with a quirky sense of humour.” Continue reading...

item.title: James McClean: ‘Wearing the poppy was just never going to happen’
item.description: The former Republic of Ireland international on growing up in a community still reeling from the Troubles and the controversy that scarred his career “The perception of me is that, basically, I am a madman,” James McClean says calmly. “I’m outspoken. I’m a loudmouth. I’m very opinionated and I hate all things British. That’s from people who don’t know me. The reality is quite the opposite. I’m pretty boring. I go training, go home and switch off. A lot of my days are quite bland, quite basic.” McClean sounds as sane as he looks gaunt on a bleak Monday in Derry. He spent 14 years in English football and the fact that he is now at war with his own club, Derry City, can’t obscure the fact that he is the fifth-most-capped Republic of Ireland international, having played 103 times. “People define success in different ways,” he says, “but I’m the only footballer from the north of Ireland to win over 100 caps for Ireland. I played 150 Premier League games over five seasons, 800 professional games and won a lot of individual accolades. I count that as success and don’t look back with regrets.” Continue reading...

item.description: Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now! There are only two things certain in life – death and taxes Reece James knack and Watford managerial news – and Football Daily’s bingo card lit up with both on Friday. But while Chelsea’s statement on their crocked right-back having successful knee surgery was a cut-and-paste job from the last time James was injured, the quotes by Watford manager Alessio Dionisi were much more exciting, mainly because it contained an actual apology to Elton John and the remarkable news that the club’s trigger-happy owners have not already sent the Italian the same way as an apple in Michael Owen’s house . Shall we just hand over the Bigger Cup to PSG now to ease the calendar congestion?” – Krishna Moorthy. Reading that ‘European football leaders are increasingly confident they will find a candidate to stand against Infantino next year’ , I can’t be the only well informed reader to think that a certain intergalactic bin wearing member of the nobility would make a terrific candidate. item.title: Football Daily | Guardiola returns to Manchester as City spin into dizzy mess against PSG
item.description: Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now! It is quite funny that PSG felt like the good guys at the Etihad Stadium but if we briefly detach ourselves from the notion that the European champions’ own sportswashing and cashsplashing has also done immeasurable damage to the beautiful game, then their 4-2 Bigger Cup shellacking of Manchester City was pure cinema, baby! I was stunned at reading the comments in support of Manchester City keeping their trophies, coming out of the mouth of their Bigger Cup rivals at PSG (yesterday’s Quote of the Day). Given the example of the organisers of the Tour de Lance … sorry, the Tour de France, this kind of ‘keep the awards you won’ stuff might get him sent to the Bastille. Or consider Formula One. They’ve got all kinds of rules about driver behaviour on the racetrack, and additional rules about what the crew can and cannot do to your car. Cars get inspected before each race, and there are also mandatory post-race inspections for every car. You might drive your car first across the line to the cheers of the crowd, but if the post-race inspection discovered that you cheated in how your team designed your vehicle, your memory of crossing the line is all you get to keep. Think about that for a minute. If the Premier League and Fifa cannot clear the bar for morals in sport set by the UCI and FIA, that says a lot. And none of it good” – Peter Rehwaldt. My friend Bernard grew up in Coventry. And as a boy he thought the team was called ‘Coventry City Nil’. I would get out more, but I’m a Manchester United fan” – Brendan Hughes. item.title: Why we’re stuck with a Premier League in the clutches of the global mega-rich | Jonathan Wilson
item.description: There’s little prospect of the model changing in a country that welcomes wealthy international owners with open arms Football, the world’s most popular sport, played by laws drawn up in London in 1863. The Premier League is the UK’s greatest soft power export. Premier League clubs are owned by a deputy prime minister of Abu Dhabi, the public investment fund of Saudi Arabia, a billionaire based in Monaco for tax reasons and a disappointing assortment of investors and private equity funds. And what, really, could be more British than that? Football truly is the national game. What the Manchester City case has exposed is just how difficult it is to regulate some of the richest and most powerful bodies in the world. While the wait for the verdict was frustrating, it was perhaps unavoidable given the possibility of legal objection at every turn when a leaked email from City’s in-house lawyer during Uefa’s action against the club had threatened to “ spend 30 million on the 50 best lawyers in the world to sue them for the next 10 years”. You didn’t get that with Albert Alexander Sr or Peter Swales. Continue reading...

item.description: From transfers to stadium works and even the training-ground dog, there is no doubting the Spaniard’s influence at the club If anyone doubts Mikel Arteta’s status as No 1 at Arsenal in the week he committed his future to the club until 2030 , just ask Win the dog. item.title: Lionel Messi’s Argentina career turned football into a sacred mystery
item.description: Jorge Messi wanted his country to fall in love with his son. That ambition was fulfilled during a brilliant international career that ended this week “What Argentina is doing in this World Cup is of a sacred order,” Brazilian writer Milly Lacombe posted at the height of the tide of anti-Argentinian sentiment during this year’s tournament. She was exploring the contradiction she felt around her support of Lionel Messi: “a player who is a God and a man who shakes Trump’s hand”. Lacombe highlighted the importance of acknowledging the complexities around Messi and the Argentinian team. How is it possible that Messi was not speaking out against the racist incidents we all saw around the Argentina team , she asked. “That’s why it hurts so much to see someone with Messi’s power choosing to make himself small,” she wrote. item.title: Next Generation 2021: why slow and steady sometimes wins the race
item.description: Our NextGen picks from five years ago show that breaking through early does not guarantee longevity or future success Read the full updates on our class of 2021 here and here In 2021, as every year, we picked 80 players from around the world who had a chance of making it in world football – 20 from the Premier League and 60 from the rest of the world – as part of our Next Generation series . We then follow these talented boys on their journeys for five years. Often it is almost impossible to predict how they will get on (OK, when Sid Lowe sent over Lamine Yamal in 2024 we had an inkling he might do well). The ball-playing central midfielder comes from a footballing family and academy staff believe his tactical awareness is born from growing up around the game. His father, Adam, played for Brighton and is now manager along the coast at Worthing FC, while Martin (his great uncle), Paul (his grandad), and Wally (his great grandad), all enjoyed careers as players. The youngest to play in the Bundesliga at 16 years and one day, youngest player to appear in the Champions League 17 days later, youngest goal scorer in Bundesliga 11 days after that and youngest player and youngest goal scorer for the Germany Under-21 team before he has turned 17. item.title: Ousmane Dembélé quietly becomes the main man after long journey to the top
item.description: The Frenchman, who has been named the best male footballer in the world by the Guardian, has benefitted from PSG’s focus on the team rather than individuals What makes a good player great, and a great player the best? This question has been occupying me since 2014, when the Guardian first asked me to contribute to its inaugural Next Generation feature . My job was to look for a France-based talent born in 1997 who could go on to have a stellar career. After a great deal of research, I narrowed it down from my shortlist of five by asking questions not about the players’ football ability, but about other attributes: resilience, adaptability, decision-making, creativity, work ethic, response to feedback and willingness to learn. Qualities we cannot see, and are harder to measure. Continue reading...
